title: Overloading, Default Arguments & inline
html:
Several functions can share a name if their parameter lists differ; the compiler picks the best match at compile time. Default arguments fill in trailing parameters.

Function overloading

RankConversion neededExample
1. Exact matchNone (or trivial: array→pointer, adding const)f(int) for f(5)
2. Promotionchar/short/bool → int, float → doublef(int) for f('c')
3. Standard conversionint → double, double → int, derived* → base*f(double) for f(5)
4. User-definedConstructor or conversion operatorf(std::string) for f("hi")
Watch out

Return type alone can't distinguish overloads, and two equally good matches are a compile error: with f(int) and f(double), calling f(5L) is ambiguous.

Default arguments

  • Defaults must be the trailing parameters: void f(int a = 1, int b); is illegal.
  • Specify them once — in the declaration (header), not again in the definition.
  • They're substituted at the call site at compile time; for virtual functions the default comes from the static type — a classic trap.

inline

inline originally meant “please paste the body at the call site”. Today compilers decide inlining themselves; the keyword's real meaning is ODR: an inline function (or C++17 inline variable) may be defined in a header included by many .cpp files without “multiple definition” link errors.

Can overloaded functions differ only by const on a by-value parameter?

No. void f(int) and void f(const int) declare the same function — top-level const on a by-value parameter isn't part of the signature. f(int&) vs f(const int&), however, are distinct overloads.

What's the difference between a macro and an inline function?

A macro is textual substitution by the preprocessor: no types, no scope, arguments may be evaluated twice (MAX(i++, j)). An inline function is a real function — type-checked, scoped, arguments evaluated once — and is optimised just as well.
